question: Does the hand-set year-over-year alerting threshold select weeks that are more likely to be the START of something, or just weeks that are anomalous?
rerun: docker exec -i station2-twin-db-1 psql -U twin -d twin -f - < platform/dataops/outbreak_alert_sweep.sql
reward_proxy: rate_next > rate (the rate rose the following week). CRUDE ON PURPOSE: a real reward needs an epidemiological definition of outbreak onset, which is a clinical judgement and not an engineering one.
finding: The deployed threshold (2.0, DRIFT_HIGH in platform/dataops/pipeline_metrics.py) selects cells that are LESS likely to keep rising (46.2%) than a cell picked at random (49.5%). Raising it 4x cuts alert volume 6.5x and moves the outcome rate only to 52.7%. The policy is selecting the SIZE of an anomaly, and a large year-over-year jump often means the peak has already arrived -- what follows a peak is a decline. It is selecting peaks, not onsets.
what_this_does_not_show: It does not show the alert is useless: a peak is worth knowing about, it is just not the same event as an onset, and the alert's name and thresholds imply onset.
The reward proxy is one week ahead and binary. Onset is a shape over several weeks.
The deployed alert (WidespreadGeoDrift) additionally requires the drift to be widespread across geographies; these numbers are the per-cell rate underneath that aggregation.
